title: Fecal microbiota transplantation in cancer immunotherapy: targeting the Gut-Tumor Axis.
authors: Yu Yue; Xu Caihua; Hua Yulin; Yang Fulin; Xie Shichang et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer therapy, but resistance and immune-related toxicities continue to limit their benefit. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) may enhance ICI efficacy and alleviate treatment-related intestinal toxicity, yet clinical responses remain inconsistent, and microbiome remodeling does not reliably predict benefit. Moreover, clinical, ecological, and mechanistic evidence remains fragmented and has not been critically integrated. This review therefore evaluates the current clinical evidence for FMT in cancer immunotherapy and examines how donor-recipient interactions, microbial engraftment and function, host immunity, and tumor context jointly shape efficacy and toxicity. We organize these mechanisms within the Gut-Tumor Axis, encompassing microbial metabolites and cellular components, cross-organ immune signaling, and intratumoral microbiota. Finally, we discuss how multi-omics and computational modeling may enable more predictable and precise microbiome interventions.

title: Clinical Utility of Nanopore-Based Targeted and Metagenomic Sequencing for Rapid Diagnosis of Infections.
authors: Lao Hiu-Yin; Hung Tin-Nok; Ng Timothy Ting-Leung; Tam Wing-Yin; Lok Tsun-Ming et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Rapid diagnosis is critical for acute invasive infections, yet conventional culture is time-consuming. The real-time, long-read capability of nanopore sequencing facilitates rapid diagnosis, but standardized workflows are lacking. Here, we describe 2 nanopore sequencing workflows, nanopore targeted sequencing (NTS) and nanopore metagenomic sequencing (NMgS), for pathogen and antimicrobial resistance identification.
METHODS: A total of 176 residual clinical specimens, of which >90% were abdominal, pleural, joint, abscess, and bile samples, were analyzed using the NTS and NMgS workflows and compared with culture. NTS employed multiplex PCR to amplify 16S rRNA gene, internal transcribed spacer region, and 30 resistance genes, while NMgS involved host DNA depletion and unbiased sequencing.
RESULTS: Among 152 culture-positive samples, NTS achieved 98.68% positivity, compared with 69.08% for NMgS. NTS identified 79.93% of cultured species, while NMgS detected 44.89%. For 24 culture-negative samples, NTS identified potential pathogens in 6 cases, whereas NMgS detected none. For antimicrobial resistance detection, NTS achieved a sensitivity of 84.62% for β-lactam resistance, 62.50% for quinolones, and 31.25% for aminoglycosides, with corresponding specificities of 87.10%, 75.86%, and 96.61%. Conversely, NMgS showed lower sensitivities of 36.84%, 16.67%, and 12.50% for these classes, while maintaining 100% specificity across all categories. Using the 4-h sequencing workflow, NTS and NMgS achieved comparable sample-to-report times (10.83 vs 10.41 h).
CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates the potential of nanopore sequencing for rapid diagnosis and provides practical insights for its implementation in clinical laboratories. While NTS is sensitive and cost-effective, NMgS offers a hypothesis-free approach. These workflows may complement routine culture in specific clinical contexts.

title: Deep longitudinal phenotyping of a single individual enables host-microbiome metabolic modeling over 3.6 years.
authors: Sheehy Anna; Martinelli Filippo; Fang Xin; Smarr Larry; Palsson Bernhard O et al.
abstract: This study examines a single subject (LS) experiencing severe episodic colonic inflammation and associated gut microbiome dysbiosis. Metagenomic sequencing of LS's stool samples at 51 time points over 3.6 years provided a time series of gut microbial species' relative abundances, from which we generated time-point specific microbiome models. Flux balance analysis was used to predict metabolic phenotypes across the time series. The microbial abundances and predicted fluxes were compared with clinical inflammation biomarkers [serum C-reactive protein (CRP); stool lactoferrin, calprotectin, lysozyme, and secretory immunoglobulin A]. Each of these 51 microbiome models were integrated with a time-point specific male whole-body metabolic model personalized based on LS's weight, blood glucose, and cholesterol. A healthy average (HeAve) community model from 34 individuals provided a reference. Our models predicted methane overproduction from high Methanobrevibacter smithii levels, coinciding with peak CRP and calprotectin. We found that Escherichia coli plays a central role in shaping the predicted metabolome and may promote inflammation through trimethylamine N-oxide and formaldehyde production, out-competing Desulfovibrio piger and Akkermansia muciniphila via active methyl and sulfur cycles. At a later time point, LS experienced a major shift in gut Proteobacteria ecology: E. coli, over-abundant at 675 × HeAve, dropped nearly 80-fold in one month, while Morganella morganii rose by nearly eight times, which coincided with a spike in LS's lactoferrin and lysozyme, a rise in species including Klebsiella pneumoniae and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a change in predicted metabolic profile, and increased alpha diversity. We also noted a correlation between postulated inflammation periods and predicted lithocholic acid levels. This work extends two previous studies of 7 and 27 of these time points. Our analysis demonstrates the value of pairing multi-omics time-series data with systems biology approaches in an n-of-1 design, resolving how microbiome composition dynamics shape host-microbiome metabolism and inflammation.
